planting.note: Plant divisions or seedlings in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil at a pond or stream margin in partial shade in spring; this hybrid swarm comes in a wide, unpredictable color range so named-strain seed batches are the best way to target a palette.

directions: Primula x bullesiana is the classic candelabra hybrid swarm between P. bulleyana and P. beesiana, producing tiered whorls of flowers that range unpredictably from butter-yellow and apricot through salmon, orange, and pink to reddish-purple on a single stem or within a single sown batch. Grow exactly as for its candelabra relatives, in permanently moist, humus-rich soil at a stream or pond margin in partial shade, since the plant collapses quickly if the root zone dries out even briefly. It self-sows readily where conditions stay wet, gradually reverting toward orange and yellow tones over generations unless replenished with fresh named-strain seed. Combine with astilbe, rodgersia, and ferns for a naturalistic waterside woodland planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring at a stream bank or bog garden; unlike the farina-dusted candelabra species it needs no special protection from leaf-wetting and tolerates somewhat heavier shade.

directions: Native to streambanks and seepage slopes in Yunnan and northern Myanmar, Primula helodoxa carries four to six tiered whorls of clear, glossy, honey-scented golden-yellow flowers on sturdy stems well above the rosette of glossy, toothed leaves in early to midsummer, slightly later than most other candelabra species. It lacks the white mealy farina coating found on P. pulverulenta and P. bulleyana, giving it a cleaner, glossier look in the border. Site it in reliably moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside a pond or stream, since it has no tolerance for drought and quickly wilts and declines in dry spells. It pairs well with blue-leaved hostas and ferns, its pure gold tone standing apart from the orange-to-crimson range of its relatives.

planting.note: Plant divisions or named-strain seedlings in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in spring; isolate from the crimson wild-type species if you want the pink color to stay true in self-sown offspring.

directions: Raised at Bartley in Hampshire, England, this long-grown seed strain of Primula pulverulenta substitutes soft shell-pink to salmon-pink flowers with a darker eye for the species' typical deep wine-crimson, while keeping the same tiered candelabra whorls and the conspicuous white mealy farina dusting the flower stalks and calyces. Grow exactly as the species, in permanently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil at a pond or stream margin in partial shade with protection from harsh midday sun. It self-seeds in suitably damp ground, but seedlings will drift back toward the crimson species color over time if grown near wild-type plants, so isolate plantings to maintain the pink strain. An excellent softer-toned companion to the deep red species and to Primula bulleyana and P. beesiana in a woodland bog garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a cool, waterside site with constant soil moisture keeps the pale color from bleaching out in strong sun.

directions: Taleggio is named for its pale, creamy, almost ivory-primrose globes, a softer and cooler tone than the gold and lemon shades of most Trollius x cultorum selections, held on compact stems above deeply cut, dark green foliage in mid to late spring. It needs the same constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade as its relatives and declines quickly in heat or drought, performing best in cool northern gardens or beside permanent water. The pale flowers combine especially well with blues and other pastels in a cool spring border, and show up well against darker-leaved companions like heuchera or dark astilbe foliage. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring or immediately after flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in early spring or immediately after flowering; this old selection needs the same constant moisture as the wild species and sulks in anything less.

directions: A long-cultivated selection of the European native globeflower dating back to Victorian-era gardens, 'Superbus' bears notably large, almost perfectly closed, deep golden-yellow globes held well above deeply palmately cut, dark green foliage in late spring. The flowers stay more fully rounded and incurved than the wild species, where sepals gape open slightly as they age, giving 'Superbus' a tidier, more formal look beside a pond or stream. Like all Trollius europaeus forms it demands cool summers and permanently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, declining fast in heat or drought and struggling above zone 7. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after the foliage dies back in late summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; deep, rich purple-red bract color develops best with consistent moisture and is less vivid in hot, dry sites.

directions: Amethyst is a richly colored masterwort selection carrying deep purple-red, almost wine-toned bracts surrounding a dome of small florets, a shade deeper and more saturated than the species but less blackish-maroon than 'Hadspen Blood'. It blooms from early summer into midsummer and often again in early autumn if spent flowering stems are sheared back after the first flush. Grow in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; it tolerates more sun than many masterworts where soil stays reliably moist, but hot, dry conditions cause the color to fade and foliage to collapse prematurely. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and flower quality.
